title: Stateless by Design
author: Sanskrati Jain
excerpt: Can a child be denied a nationality because of their parents' immigration status? This article examines the gaps in India's citizenship framework and explores the legal reforms needed to prevent statelessness.
content:
Children must not suffer for their parents’ lack of documentation. Unfortunately, this is the case in India. A child born in India is protected by neither the Citizenship Act, 1955 (“Act”) nor by certain international frameworks such as Convention on the Rights of the Child (“CRC”). This is not merely a consequence of a gap in implementation; rather, it reflects the legal position under Indian law. However, this does not apply to every child born in India. It specifically affects children born to an "illegal migrant," as defined under the Act.
What Does the Law Say?
Since 2003, Section 3(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act, 1955 demands that a child born in India must be born to parents that are both Indian citizens or one that is an Indian citizen and other that is not an “illegal migrant”.  Additionally, a proviso inserted in Section 2(1)(b) of the Act through an amendment in 2019 categorically excludes children of Muslim migrants from obtaining citizenship.  An “illegal migrant” as defined in Section 2(1)(b) of the Act is a person that has either entered the country without authorised documents such as a valid passport or with valid documents but continues to reside beyond permitted duration.  
In situations where citizenship is in question, it becomes important to consult not only domestic but also international legal standards. Indian law treats citizenship as a right to be inherited and not an immediate entitlement upon birth.  Article 7 of the CRC, on the other hand explicitly accords a child with the right to a nationality immediately upon birth.  The same provision ensures that a child remains protected, stating that parties to the convention must abide by and effectively implement the obligations to the convention particularly when a child may be rendered stateless due to discrepancies in domestic law. India accepted the obligation of the right to a nationality in 1992 but did not ratify a specific enforcement or redressal system for the same. The 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons seeks to ensure non-discrimination on grounds of race, religion or country of origin.  The 1961 Convention on Reduction of Statelessness obligates parties to create protections to prevent statelessness at birth and later in life and providing nationality to children born in countries where they would otherwise be rendered stateless.

The CRC together with the 1954 and 1961 conventions would provide for a seamless protection and redressal system for children born in India that could be rendered stateless due to domestic law. However, India is not a party to either the 1954 Convention or the 1961 Convention. This creates a legal vacuum for children born in such unfortunate circumstances, wherein each legal framework is internally coherent and defensible on its own terms and so, children who fall within this gap are left without effective protection. The issue is that for a child born in India to a parent that is an “illegal migrant” there is no single institution that can be individually held responsible, and this creates a harder battle for the child to defend his or her right to acquire a nationality.  
 The most practical solution lies within the Act itself. Section 5 already permits citizenship by registration for specific categories of persons, including minor children of Indian citizens,  and this same mechanism could be extended to children who would otherwise be rendered stateless under Section 3(1)(c) . This does not require inventing a new legislative framework, only widening an existing one to a population currently excluded from it. Complete ratification of the 1961 Convention, with its broad obligation to grant nationality in most circumstances, may not be a step India is prepared to take, particularly for a country managing a population of 1.4 billion, but a registration pathway carries none of that structural risk and addresses the same issue at its root. Ratifying the 1954 Convention would remain a useful complementary step, ensuring that children who fall through the cracks are at least treated with dignity and free from discrimination, but it cannot substitute for a domestic mechanism that prevents statelessness at birth in the first place.
Ultimately, this issue extends beyond inconsistencies in the law. It concerns identity, belonging, dignity, and legal security for children. No child should have to go through battles of nationality throughout their childhood and later adulthood, protections must exist and if they fail, clearly established redressal systems must be there to secure the child.[1] Citizenship Act, No.57 of 1955, § 3(1)(c) (India).
